thread.title: The Dow Hits a Record High as Tech Sits It Out

author: Ben Levisohn
title: The Dow Hits a Record High as Tech Sits It Out
text:
David Byrne in Talking Heads’ 1984 film "Stop Making Sense." Photo: Cinecom Pictures By Ben Levisohn Sept. 21, 2018 9:39 p.m. ET In Talking Heads’ 1984 concert film Stop Making Sense, the band merged the ridiculous—frontman David Byrne’s oversize suits—with the sublime. That might also be the best way to describe the market this past week, which didn’t always make sense but sure left many feeling good.
We thought the market needed tech to have a good week. It proved it didn’t. The Nasdaq Composite dropped 0.3%, to 7986.96, as large components like Amazon.com (ticker: AMZN) and Apple (AAPL) finished lower. But the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 588.83 points, or 2.3%, to 26,743.50—a record close—and the S&P 500, which rose 0.8%, to 2929.67, narrowly missed a record of its own. It was a thing of beauty…unless you were overweight the FAANGs.
Then there was the strange relationship between the U.S. dollar and the 10-year Treasury yield. When the yield goes up, the dollar usually does, too, as the extra payout makes it more attractive. But that’s not what happened this past week. The yield on the 10-year Treasury rose 0.076 percentage point, to 3.068%, and closed at the sixth-highest level of the year, but the U.S. Dollar index fell 0.8%, its second consecutive weekly decline.
Those moves make more sense if viewed in terms of changing risk perception, says Deutsche Bank strategist Alan Ruskin. When investors are scared that something bad will happen, they buy both dollars and Treasuries; when they’re feeling more relaxed, they sell both to buy riskier assets.
One need only look overseas for a sign that investors are feeling better about the state of the world—or at least better enough to do some bargain-hunting. China’s Shanghai Composite rose 4.3% this past week, though it is still down 21% from its January high, while the iShares MSCI Emerging Markets exchange-traded fund (EEM) rose 3%.
Of course, rising interest rates were one of the reasons given for the February correction, but right now they’re viewed as a reflection of a stronger economy, not something to be feared. Ruskin expects that to remain the case as long yields remain below 3.13%, their May intraday high. When they cross that level, he says, “yields will matter again.”
Rising yields could be signaling a more lasting shift away from tech stocks, contends Fundstrat Global Advisors’ Thomas Lee. He observes that just three S&P 500 sectors have outperformed the broader index, something that has happened only eight times since 1926. (This time around, the sectors are information technology, consumer discretionary, and health care.) In the past, when such a narrow slice of the market carries all that weight, up years tend to be followed by down years—and the weakness is concentrated in the previous year’s winners.
One thing that could turn this year’s winners into losers: higher yields. “The rise of the 10-year yield above 3% may signal a change in leadership,” Lee writes.
Maybe it all makes sense, after all.
